subtitle: Wednesday, 9 September 2026
editor_note: This edition brings together developments that touch several parts of Tamkeen's mandate: the effect of AI on young people and learning, new support for skills and journalism, the changing nature of work, and the rise of nationally-owned 'sovereign' AI. We also include a sober note on AI safety, where researchers themselves are voicing serious concerns. Together these stories show both the opportunities AI offers for human-capital development and the responsibilities that come with adopting it.

items.title: Funding grants for new research into AI and teen development
items.summary: OpenAI has opened applications for a $5 million grant program funding independent research into how generative AI affects teenagers. The program will support studies on adolescent development, well-being, and safety, aiming to build evidence about the benefits and risks of AI for young users. This matters because much of today's discussion about AI and children is based on limited data, and independent research could inform better guidance for parents, schools, and policymakers. For an institution focused on education and human capital, the findings could eventually shape how AI tools are introduced responsibly to young learners. The initiative also reflects a broader push by AI companies to fund external scrutiny of their products' social effects.

items.title: OpenAI expands initiatives to support journalism from classrooms to newsrooms
items.summary: OpenAI announced an expansion of its support for journalism, spanning from classrooms to professional newsrooms. The effort includes tools, training, and partnerships aimed at students, educators, working journalists, and news organizations to help them use AI responsibly in their work. The goal is to build practical AI skills across the media pipeline, from those learning the craft to established outlets. For Tamkeen, this is a concrete example of how AI training and upskilling are being tailored to a specific profession rather than offered generically. It also highlights ongoing questions about how AI intersects with accurate information and the future of media work.

items.title: The Work Now Within Reach
items.summary: In a piece titled 'The Work Now Within Reach,' OpenAI argues that AI is becoming both more capable and more affordable, allowing people and businesses to take on tasks that were previously too costly or complex. The central message is that cheaper, stronger AI tools could expand the range of work individuals can accomplish and make economic growth more attainable. While the framing comes from a company promoting its own technology, the underlying trend is relevant to workforce planning everywhere. As AI lowers the cost of certain tasks, the skills people need and the way jobs are designed may shift. For workforce-development bodies, this reinforces the importance of helping employees adapt to tools that change what is possible in their roles.

items.title: Mistral raises €3B as sovereign AI becomes big business
items.summary: French AI company Mistral has raised €3 billion in new funding at a €21 billion valuation, in a round led by Samsung, Scaleup Europe, and PSG Equity. The investment reflects growing interest in 'sovereign AI' — the idea that countries and regions want AI systems developed and controlled within their own borders rather than relying entirely on a few large foreign providers. Mistral, seen as Europe's leading challenger to American AI firms, benefits from governments and companies seeking greater independence and data control. This trend is directly relevant to the Gulf, where the UAE and neighbours are also investing in home-grown AI capabilities. The scale of the funding shows that national and regional AI ambitions are now attracting very large amounts of capital.

items.title: Worried Anthropic researchers warn that AI ‘could kill all humans’
items.summary: A senior safety researcher at Anthropic, a leading AI company, has publicly stated there is more than a 10 percent chance that AI 'could kill all humans' by the end of the decade. The warning came shortly after a colleague resigned, citing concerns that AI labs and their competitors are recklessly racing to build 'superhuman systems' they cannot reliably control. These are unusually stark statements coming from inside the industry itself, rather than from outside critics. While such predictions are debated and uncertain, they underline why AI safety, governance, and responsible development are receiving serious attention worldwide. For public-sector institutions, they reinforce the value of careful, well-governed adoption of AI rather than rushing to deploy the most powerful systems.
